item.title: 🔵 How BCG turns client innovation into enterprise AI
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Most CIOs deploy technology created by vendors or developed internally for their own organizations. At Boston Consulting Group, CIO Merim Becirovic operates in a different environment. Every day, the firm’s consultants help clients across industries rethink business processes, redesign operating models, and explore new applications of AI. That gives him and his team visibility into a constant stream of experimentation and innovation happening beyond BCG’s walls.

Rather than viewing those ideas as client work alone, Becirovic embraces the concept of customer zero, applying the most promising capabilities within BCG itself. The result is a powerful feedback loop: client engagements generate new ideas, BCG tests and refines them internally, and the lessons learned strengthen future client work.

In this conversation, Becirovic discusses how BCG scales AI through its Genie platform, gives employees the freedom to experiment safely, and turns emerging ideas into the transformation of how work gets done.

item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

Death, taxes and cyber incidents. It’s not quite the original saying, but for today’s CISO, all three carry a certain inevitability, and most organizations have come to accept that reality.

Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study confirms that cybersecurity remains the top investment priority for CISOs. Yet even well-funded security programs can struggle when something goes wrong.

Why? The cause is rarely missing plans or controls; it’s silos. Service owners; security, recovery and crisis teams; and key providers too often plan and operate apart. As a result, organizations are beginning to see that investment and resilience are not the same thing.

item.title: 🟠 Your agentic AI results can’t be checked. Here’s how to fix that
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

Read 50 published accounts of agentic AI in production and a pattern emerges fast. Escalations down. Handling times down. Conversion up. Onboarding compressed from weeks to days.

Now read them looking for how those numbers were produced, and the field thins out. The window is rarely stated, the denominator almost never and concurrent initiatives that could have produced the same movement go unnamed. You get a number and an implied causal claim, with nothing a skeptic could object to.

This usually isn’t dishonesty. Nobody has told practitioners what a defensible result looks like, so careful and careless accounts read identically.

The cost lands on CIOs. If you’re weighing a major agentic investment, you can’t tell a result achieved at peak trading volume from one achieved in a quiet quarter with the window picked afterward. Both show up as a percentage.

item.description:

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has made it untenable for software vendors to sit on privately reported flaws for months, and Google Project Zero is responding by shrinking its vulnerability disclosure deadline from 90 to 60 days, with plans to drop it to 30 days a year from now. Anthropic is following suit with an even more aggressive timeline.

item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

Nearly every cyber recovery plan relies on assumptions about how recovery will unfold. Teams expect incidents can be fully contained before recovery begins, that recovery can proceed in a mostly linear sequence, and that they will have sufficient visibility into system and data dependencies.

Destructive cyberattacks can quickly challenge those assumptions. The 2026 Cohesity Global Cyber Resilience Report found that among organizations that experienced a material cyberattack in the previous 12 months, 70% saw the scope of affected systems expand beyond the initial assessment, 61% identified moderate or significant gaps in how their plans accounted for dependencies, and 76% exceeded their recovery time objectives, with recovery taking nearly twice as long as planned.

item.title: 🟠 The AI deregulation illusion: Why CIOs face more rules, not fewer
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

If you follow the headlines coming out of Washington, you might conclude that AI regulation is on its way out. The administration has made reducing regulatory barriers a priority, arguing that lighter oversight is essential to American innovation and competitiveness. But for CIOs responsible for deploying AI across large enterprises, the reality is exactly the opposite.

While Washington pushes for fewer restrictions, states are passing new AI legislation, international regulators are enforcing increasingly complex requirements, and lawmakers are turning their attention to how businesses actually use AI. Essentially, while AI may be getting deregulated at the federal level, it’s becoming more regulated in practice.

For organizations operating across state and national borders, this creates an increasingly difficult challenge. An AI application that meets requirements in one jurisdiction may trigger additional obligations in another. And as AI becomes embedded in more business-critical processes, the consequences of inadequate governance are growing.

At 09:24 on a quiet Tuesday, an AI agent spots suspicious privileged activity. It concludes the safest move is to turn off the identity service. So it does.

Everything works as designed. The agent has its own identity. Its credentials are scoped. The action lands in a log nobody can alter. The policy was clear enough: don’t interrupt production services without approval. The agent read the policy, weighed the threat and decided containment counted as approval.

By 09:30, the call centre can’t log in. Neither can the payments team.

Three good executives arrive in the same room with three different instincts. The CIO wants the service back. The CISO wants it kept down until someone proves the threat has gone. The CRO is doing quieter arithmetic, working out how long the firm can limp before it breaches a tolerance the board signed off last spring.

item.title: 🔵 Cloud repatriation is on the rise — but tricky questions remain
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

Enterprises are moving to the cloud faster than they have in years. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of IT decision-makers say their organizations sped up cloud migration over the past 12 months, according to Foundry’s 2026 Cloud Computing Study.

Yet a growing number are also bringing some workloads back in-house. About two-thirds (66%) say their organizations have moved or plan to move workloads out of public cloud.

“Repatriation is one part of a wider rethink of where workloads belong,” says Mukesh Ranjan, vice president at Everest Group, a research and advisory firm.

AI workloads are part of the calculus. They’re leaving public cloud nearly as often as storage and databases, and just 13% of IT decision-makers plan to run AI primarily there, according to Foundry’s research. For CIOs, that means deciding workload by workload where each one belongs, with AI adding new factors to weigh, from GPU costs to where models run and where prompts are processed.

item.title: 🔵 The illusion of AI productivity in software development and what to measure instead
item.description:
Why this matters: Leadership context — useful for risk, budget, vendor, and strategic conversations.

Accenture reports that 82% of C-suite leaders are increasing AI investments, signaling continued confidence in the technology. But if you talk to tech leaders, the returns aren’t so clear-cut. AI can write code in seconds, but that’s only the first stage of software development. When AI-generated output introduces errors, misses internal requirements or requires extensive rework, the time saved upfront can quickly disappear.

A report from Bain & Co validates this — AI coding tools are helping developers complete roughly 21% more tasks, but time spent reviewing outputs rose 91%. As engineers generate more code, senior developers face growing review queues. AI can also produce lengthy specifications and documentation that take time to evaluate. This obscures the impact AI adoption is having on the software development lifecycle and, much of the time, simply creates more work.

item.title: 🔵 Mitigate memory price increases with components harvested from retiring devices
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

The circular economy just picked up one of its strongest business cases yet, and it didn’t come from a sustainability mandate. It came from a memory shortage. An AI-induced memory shortage has pushed the price of new devices up, causing organizations to recalculate their repair-vs-replace threshold, and to look again at what a decommissioned device is still worth.

Rather than proceeding with typical 3 to 4-year refresh cycles, many IT and procurement teams have shifted to preservation mode, holding devices longer where they can and stretching the cycle. Another trend gaining ground: internal component harvesting. Instead of treating retiring or broken laptops as something to dispose of, forward-thinking organizations are treating them as sub-component mines. This means pulling the working memory and graphics cards out of a device too old to redeploy, and putting them into devices that can.

Procurement can buy memory at the new price, or pull it from a device it just decommissioned. The rest of this article covers the three main steps that make the second option work.

item.title: 🔵 Ghost businesses are easier to build than ever
item.description:
Why this matters: Endpoint-security changes may affect detection and alerting.

Earlier this year, CBS News reporters set out to investigate 89 licensed hospice companies. The task was simpler than it seemed at first glance: state records tied these companies to a single, 32,000-square-foot Los Angeles building that also housed a salon, a law office and a modeling agency. The building’s owner said only 12 were still there. The gap between the business registry and on-the-ground reality was clearly a problem.

When I saw that story, I did what any curious technologist in my position would do; I started thinking about finding those ghost businesses automatically using modern data analysis techniques. I turned our tools loose on it.

Trulioo’s business data covers more than 100 million U.S. business records, and its value here is in how those records connect. Linking each company to its directors, addresses and owners turns a registry into a map. item.title: 🔵 Building AI-enabled cities starts with putting people first
item.description:
Why this matters: Hospitality-system impact — consider guest services, PMS/POS, and property operations.

The cities getting the most out of AI aren’t just the ones adopting it fastest but those putting their residents first. These cities are seeing more than twice the return on their AI investments compared with their peers. This is according to ThoughtLab’s new global report, Building a People-First, AI-Powered City.

The research is based on a survey of 525 senior officials across 215 cities worldwide, alongside a review of 363 city AI plans. The report found a clear link between how cities approach AI and what they get in return. It also identified 37 AI leaders that combine technology with strong governance, workforce development, citizen engagement and human-centred design.

Mark Wittenburg, Raleigh’s CIO, participated in the study and was part of the report advisory board. item.description:

This summer, the maintainers of vm2, an open-source JavaScript sandboxing library with 1 million downloads per week, shipped fixes for 34 separate sandbox-escape vulnerabilities and Anthropic’s Claude co-wrote 19 of them. Weeks later, a security researcher pointed an AI agent at one of the advisories and asked for a way around the patch. The agent delivered.

Shayaun Nejad, lead product security engineer at Rubrik, ran vulnerability variant analysis on the vm2 patch while preparing for a talk he held at the recent [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. He wanted to highlight the challenges his development team faced when dealing with a flood of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and noted that the same bugs kept being rediscovered later in new testing runs despite being fixed by AI-assisted pipelines.

item.description:

A firewall is intended to be a boundary attackers can’t cross.

But firewalls face the web, making them just as vulnerable to attack as other systems, as evidenced by the emergency hotfixes released by Check Point Software for several of its products. item.title: 🔴 Thousands of GitHub repos hit with secret-stealing malware
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Researchers have uncovered a campaign in which hijacked GitHub accounts spread secret-stealing malware across thousands of repositories. The payload executed in at least 1,806 repos, exfiltrating CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials.

Aikido Security, which detected and documented the campaign, said the attackers used the 4,837 compromised accounts to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories starting Nov. 10. Around 92% of those pull requests, titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” are still open, which suggests most project owners have not seen them.

However, the probes on their own are benign and were performed only to check whether the hijacked accounts had write-access in those repos so that the attackers could follow up with commits that contained the malicious payload: a 1,500-line shell script that collects GitHub Actions secrets, cloud credentials, and API keys for AI services and developer tools.

item.title: 🔴 How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

AI may be helping cyberattackers increase the speed and scale of their operations, but it is not yet changing their core objectives or the techniques they employ as part of their attack chains.

Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively unskilled attackers, according to security experts.

“Attackers are still identifying targets, performing reconnaissance, establishing a foothold, moving laterally, achieving their objective, covering their tracks, and moving on to the next target,” says Ronald Lewis, director of cybersecurity governance at application security firm Black Duck. “What’s changed is the volume and velocity that AI allows this process to happen.”

item.description:

On the morning of Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down within a few hours of one another. OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. Service was back by early afternoon, and most of the coverage focused on people who couldn’t write, code or research for a morning.

An active threat campaign is combining port scanning, password guessing, and Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands to compromise exposed Microsoft SQL servers and deliver malware.

The attackers are using predefined username and password lists to brute-force into these servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems.

item.title: 🟠 AI found Linux kernel bugs that remained undetected for decades
item.description:
Why this matters: Privilege-escalation risk — review local admin and endpoint controls.

A Microsoft research project combining AI agents with human security researchers uncovered 59 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including bugs that had survived in production code for more than 20 years.

While AI dramatically accelerated the discovery process, the researchers found that validating flaws, developing patches, and working with maintainers remained overwhelmingly human-intensive.

The research, conducted by Microsoft’s FORGE Lab under the codename MDASH, generated 26,502 potential findings in approximately two weeks of scanning selected Linux kernel subsystems. Automated screening, proof-of-concept testing, and human validation narrowed these down to 59 public upstream reports, Microsoft said in a blog post.

“We developed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline,” the researchers said in the blog post.…

item.title: 🟠 The developer laptop just became production. Now what?
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. Testing also assumed that software would behave predictably when executed again.

Coding agents are upending both assumptions. Developers now run autonomous software on laptops containing GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials and authenticated browser sessions. They’re connecting agents to MCP servers, granting access to repositories and services, and copying suggested commands into terminals without always understanding what those commands will do. When permission prompts become an obstacle, it’s tempting to click through them or enable unrestricted access. Developers are inventing security policies on the fly.

Railway said the attacker’s database searches looked for AI provider keys by name before anything else; some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials.
